analysis.investment_thesis: Capri Global Capital has delivered remarkable revenue growth at 37% CAGR over nine years, but the business model requires constantly borrowing more money to grow its loan book, resulting in operating cash outflows every single year for five consecutive years, D/E of 2.52, and finance costs exploding at 68% CAGR — the classic pattern of a leveraged NBFC growing aggressively just before a potential credit cycle turn.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR of 37.2% and net profit CAGR of 30.4% over nine years represent genuinely exceptional business expansion from a small base
Forward P/E of 12.96x and improving profitability (INR 479 Cr net profit in FY25 vs INR 205 Cr in FY23) suggest the market has not fully priced in the near-term earnings ramp
High promoter holding of 59.92% and strong DII ownership of 20.09% indicate insider confidence and institutional conviction
key_risks: D/E of 2.52 is dangerously high — total debt of INR 15,577 Cr against equity of INR 6,673 Cr means any deterioration in asset quality will rapidly erode the equity base
Finance costs have grown from INR 12 Cr (FY16) to INR 1,274 Cr (FY25) at a 68% CAGR — this is a business increasingly owned by its creditors, not its shareholders
ROE of only 11.8% despite 37% revenue CAGR reveals that the rapid growth is destroying economics on a per-rupee-of-equity basis — scale has not improved returns
red_flags: Operating cash flow negative in all five of the last five years, totalling roughly INR -13,000 Cr in cumulative outflows — this is a business that consumes, not generates, cash
Total assets nearly doubled in one year (INR 15,150 Cr in FY24 to INR 24,413 Cr in FY25) — this pace of balance sheet expansion is a hallmark of aggressive credit cycles that often end badly
P/S of 7.2x for an NBFC with 11.8% ROE implies the market is paying a premium that requires everything to go right: credit quality, interest rates, competition, and regulation
analysis.detailed_analysis:
I have a deep wariness of financial companies that grow their loan books rapidly using borrowed money. Capri Global is a textbook example — every year it borrows more than it collected from operations the prior year, relying on external financing to fund the next tranche of loans. This works spectacularly well in an up-cycle and fails catastrophically in a downturn. The consistent negative operating cash flows are not a quirk of accounting; they reflect the core reality that this company is a conduit of other people's money, not a generator of its own.

The NBFC space in India — home loans, MSME loans, gold loans — is intensely competitive, with HDFC, Bajaj Finance, Muthoot, and hundreds of regional players. I see no durable moat here. The 37% revenue CAGR is impressive, but at a ROE of 11.8% after all that growth, the business is not earning extraordinary returns on capital. When the credit cycle turns, leveraged NBFCs with rapid expansion history are invariably the hardest hit. I learned this lesson watching financial crises globally — rapid credit growth funded by cheap debt is a warning signal, not a growth story.
